subject: 우르 왕묘의 순장
title: Graves that held more than one person
content: When excavators opened the royal graves at Ur in the nineteen twenties, they found something they had not expected. Alongside the principal occupant lay dozens of other bodies, arranged in rows, dressed in ornament and accompanied by instruments, weapons, and wagons. This ancient cemetery has been argued about ever since. The excavator concluded that attendants had followed their ruler into the grave, taking a drink and lying down in place, and that reading held for many decades. It rested partly on the orderly arrangement, since the bodies showed no sign of struggle and their positions suggested arrangement rather than collapse. Later study revised the account. Examination of several skulls with modern imaging revealed fractures consistent with a blow, and traces of heating and of mercury suggested that bodies had been treated to slow decay while the burial proceeded. So the deaths were probably neither peaceful nor simultaneous, and the ceremony extended over a considerable period rather than a single afternoon. What the graves record about that civilization is a claim about rank. A ruler whose household follows them into the earth is being presented as something other than a very rich person, and the labour involved in the whole event was enormous. Such practice appears in several ancient societies at a particular stage, and it tends to disappear as states become larger and more bureaucratic. The material itself is remarkable. Gold, lapis carried from the mountains far to the east, and carnelian from the Indus region all appear, which places this city within an exchange network spanning thousands of kilometres in the third millennium before our era. What the burials therefore supply is two kinds of evidence at once: a picture of how power presented itself, and a map of how far the goods that displayed it had travelled.

subject: 이집트 서기의 훈련
title: Learning to write in an ancient bureaucracy
content: Ancient Egypt ran on written records, and producing the people who kept them required a long training. Texts used in that training survive in some number, mostly on pottery fragments and limestone flakes that pupils used because papyrus was expensive, and they show what the education actually consisted of. Copying was the method of this ancient school. Pupils wrote out standard compositions again and again, and the surviving flakes carry the same passages in hands ranging from clumsy to assured. Errors were corrected in a second hand, so the sheets record teaching rather than merely practice. Because the same texts were copied across centuries, works composed in one era survived into much later ones through the schoolroom rather than through any library. The content of these ancient exercises was not neutral. A famous composition lists the miseries of every other occupation — the potter caked in clay, the fisherman among crocodiles, the soldier beaten and marched — and concludes that the scribe alone is spared. Pupils copied this repeatedly, so the training instilled an identity along with a skill, and the profession's sense of its own standing is visible in the very exercises that produced it. Two ancient scripts had to be learned. The formal signs carved on monuments differed considerably from the cursive hand used for daily accounts, and a working scribe needed the second far more than the first. Advanced students added older forms of the language, since religious texts preserved a stage of the language that ordinary speech had left behind, much as later scholars elsewhere learned an ancient tongue for the same reason. What this civilization built through that training was an administration that could tax, measure, and record across a long river valley for thousands of years. The pupils complaining on their limestone flakes were being fitted into a machine whose durability is among the more remarkable facts of ancient history.

subject: 미케네 선문자의 해독
title: Breaking a script that hid a known language
content: Clay tablets from the palaces of ancient Greece carried a script that nobody could read for half a century after its discovery. It had been assumed to record an unknown language, since it was found in a civilization that preceded the Greek alphabet by centuries and was destroyed long before the classical era. The assumption was wrong, and overturning it is among the more instructive episodes in the history of decipherment. The work on these ancient tablets proceeded without any bilingual key. Instead the decipherer built grids relating signs by their behaviour, noting which endings varied where a word appeared in different grammatical positions, and which signs occurred only at the beginnings of words. This produced a structure of relationships before any sign had a sound attached, so the method resembled solving a puzzle about pattern rather than reading. The breakthrough came from ancient place names. If certain frequently occurring words were the names of towns in the region, and if those towns had kept their names into the classical era, then the sound values could be tested. When the values were applied, Greek words appeared — for chariot wheels, for sheep, for quantities of grain — and the tablets turned out to be inventories in a very early form of the language. What these ancient records contain disappointed some. They are administrative records rather than literature: lists of stores, of workers, of offerings, and of equipment. Yet the disappointment was misplaced, since these lists supply an account of how a palace of that era actually operated, naming occupations, ranks, and holdings that no later source preserves. The lesson for the field was that assumptions do the most damage when nobody notices them. The script was unreadable for fifty years partly because everybody agreed in advance about which language it could not be recording.

subject: 에트루리아 무덤 벽화
title: Painted tombs of a people we hear about from their rivals
content: The Etruscans held much of central Italy before Rome grew large, and almost everything written about them survives in the words of the Romans who absorbed them. Their own literature is lost. What remains, besides inscriptions that can be read phonetically but understood only in part, is a body of painted tombs cut into soft rock. The paintings show banquets. Men and women recline together on couches, servants carry vessels, musicians play, and dancers move between the tables, and the scenes are rendered in bright flat colour across whole chamber walls. Because such images were made for the dead rather than for display, they were not intended as public statements, which is precisely what makes them useful as evidence about how this ancient civilization pictured a good life. One detail attracted particular attention from Roman writers. Women appear at these banquets as participants rather than as attendants, reclining alongside men, and Roman authors of a later era mention Etruscan women with disapproval that reveals more about Rome than about Etruria. The tombs support the observation while removing the moral judgment attached to it, and inscriptions naming mothers as well as fathers point the same way. Dating the paintings has allowed a sequence to be constructed. Earlier chambers show celebration; later ones, made as the cities were falling under Roman control, show demons and journeys to an underworld, and the shift in mood across roughly two centuries is unmistakable. What survives is therefore a civilization known mainly through its graves. The cities were built over, the books were not copied, and the language faded, and yet the walls of the tombs preserve a self portrait that the written record, composed by the winners, would never have supplied.

subject: 알렉산드리아 도서관의 실체
title: What the famous library actually was
content: The library at Alexandria occupies a large place in the popular picture of the ancient world, usually as a single great building destroyed in a catastrophe that set back knowledge by centuries. Nearly every element of that picture is doubtful, and reconstructing what the institution was requires setting the story aside. This library was part of a larger ancient foundation attached to the royal palace, and its members were supported to study and to write. Ancient sources describe an effort to acquire copies of every work available, with agents purchasing manuscripts abroad and ships entering the harbour required to surrender any books aboard for copying. Whether the numbers reported are reliable is doubtful, since ancient figures of this kind were rarely counted. Its most important product was scholarly rather than architectural, and these methods outlived the building itself. Working with many copies of the same text, scholars there developed methods for comparing versions, marking suspect lines, and producing an edition — practices that underlie textual scholarship still. The division of long works into books, and much of the punctuation and accentuation of Greek, came out of this environment. No single destruction accounts for its loss. Fire during a Roman siege damaged part of the holdings, later civil disturbance destroyed more, and the institution declined through the withdrawal of royal funding and the departure of scholars over generations. The dramatic version, in which one deliberate act extinguished ancient learning, appears in sources written long afterwards and serves whichever party the author wished to blame. What the case illustrates is how institutions actually fail. Loss of support, loss of people, and the slow decay of unread manuscripts destroy a library as thoroughly as any fire, and far less visibly, which is why the story preferred by later ages is the one with a villain in it.

subject: 로마 수도교의 경사
title: Water carried by a fall you cannot see
content: Roman aqueducts of the ancient empire moved water across long distances using gravity alone, and the problem they solved was one of extreme precision. Water flowing too steeply scours the channel and arrives faster than the city can take it; water flowing too gently deposits sediment and stops. The gradient had to sit between those failures across many kilometres. Surveys of surviving lines show falls of remarkably small size. One well studied aqueduct in southern Gaul descends only about a third of a metre per kilometre across its middle section, which required the builders to hold a level over ground they could not see along. The instrument used was a simple frame with plumb lines and sights, and the accuracy achieved with it across fifty kilometres is the achievement rather than the arches. The arches are the visible part of these ancient works and were the exception. Most of these channels ran underground or along the contour of hillsides, and bridges were built only where a valley had to be crossed, since raising the whole line on masonry would have been ruinously expensive. The famous structures therefore represent the difficult stretches rather than the ordinary method. Maintenance shaped their design across the centuries. Access shafts at intervals allowed workers to enter and clear the deposit that hard water leaves, and thick layers of that deposit in surviving channels record centuries of flow and of neglect. Where the crust grew thick enough to narrow the channel, capacity fell, so the system depended on continuous labour that a stable administration supplied. What the ruins of this ancient civilization record is therefore not merely construction but institution. The stone survived the empire; the arrangements that kept the channels clear did not, and several cities that had been supplied for centuries went back to wells within a generation of the administration failing.

subject: 한대 화상석이 그린 일상
title: Carved stones that show an ancient day
content: Tombs of the Han period in China were frequently lined with stone slabs carved in low relief, and the scenes on them are among the fullest pictures of daily life surviving from that ancient civilization. Because they were made for the dead, they record what a family wished to carry forward rather than what an official record would preserve. The subjects are strikingly ordinary alongside the ceremonial ones. Kitchens appear with cooks at work, hunters shoot birds from a lake, farmers plough with an ox, and travellers ride in carriages of a type no text describes in enough detail to reconstruct. Craft processes appear as well, including a well documented scene of salt production showing a derrick, pipes carrying brine, and pans over fires, which is the principal evidence for how that industry worked. Entertainment is prominent. Acrobats, jugglers, musicians, and dancers occupy whole slabs, and their presence indicates what a household of some standing expected to enjoy. The carvings therefore supply information about music, instruments, and performance that no surviving text of the era conveys, since writing of that period concerned itself with government and philosophy rather than with amusement. Mythological subjects share the same walls. Figures associated with immortality, with the sun and moon, and with a paradise mountain appear alongside the kitchens, and the mixture is not confusion. The programme presents a whole world, in which the ordinary and the divine occupy one continuous space, and the deceased passes between them. Reading these stones requires care, since a scene chosen for a tomb was chosen for a purpose and may show an ideal rather than a practice. Even so, the details of tools, dress, and posture had to be recognisable to those who commissioned them, and it is in those details that the evidence lies.

subject: 역학 조사와 개인 정보
title: Tracing an outbreak through people's lives
content: Stopping an outbreak requires knowing who was infected, where they went, and whom they met. Gathering that record is intrusive by design, since its value depends on detail, and the moral question is what may be demanded and under what conditions. Two real claims collide here, and neither can simply be waved away. The public claim is strong. An infected person moving among others imposes a risk they never consented to, and tracing contacts prevents harm that no individual choice could prevent. Where a disease is serious and spreading, the case for compelling disclosure resembles other situations in which liberty yields to a demonstrable danger. The private claim is equally real. A record of where somebody went reveals far more than disease: who they see, what they believe, other illnesses, and things they may have good reason to keep to themselves. Publishing such traces has cost people employment and safety in documented cases, so the harm is not merely feared. Justice asks who bears that cost, since it falls on those already ill. Several principles narrow the dispute considerably. Whatever is gathered for an outbreak should serve that purpose alone and be destroyed afterwards, since retaining it converts a temporary measure into a standing power. What is told to the public should be as little as will do, because warning people rarely calls for naming anyone. And such powers should lapse by their own terms rather than wait on a later choice to give them up. What history suggests is that the last principle matters most. Emergency measures are adopted quickly and surrendered slowly, and a capacity built for a genuine crisis remains available for purposes nobody debated. The moral case for gathering it is often sound; the moral case for keeping it almost never is.

subject: 실크로드 오아시스 도시
title: Towns that existed because the desert had water
content: The routes linking China with the west did not cross open desert in a straight line. They ran between oases, each fed by water descending from mountains, and the towns at those points were the reason the whole system worked. Caravans could travel only as far as the next reliable water, so the spacing of springs determined the shape of the ancient network. These ancient towns grew wealthy on service rather than on production. They supplied fodder, lodging, animals, guides, and a market where goods changed hands, and much of the trade proceeded in stages, with commodities passing through many hands rather than travelling the whole distance with one merchant. Consequently a Chinese silk reaching Rome had crossed a chain of transactions, and few people involved had any picture of both ends. Such towns became meeting points for more than goods, and each held a small civilization of its own. Excavation at several sites has produced documents in a remarkable number of scripts and languages, along with religious material from traditions that originated thousands of kilometres apart. Buddhist, Manichaean, Christian, and Zoroastrian texts have been recovered from the same region, and monasteries carved into cliffs near these settlements served travellers as well as residents. Their fate through the medieval centuries depended on water and on rule together. Where a stream shifted or an irrigation system failed, a town could be abandoned within a generation, and several are now buried under sand with their buildings standing. Where the routes moved, because sea transport became cheaper or because a frontier closed, prosperity ended even though the water remained. What survives is a chain of ruins preserving material that the damp climates of the destinations destroyed. The dry sand of this ancient region has kept paper, cloth, and paint intact for a thousand years, which is why so much of what is known about the exchange comes from its middle rather than from either end.

subject: 독점이 나쁜 이유
title: What is actually wrong with a single seller
content: The standard objection to monopoly is economic: a single seller restricts output and raises price, so buyers pay more and less is produced than would be. This is correct and it is not the whole moral case, since several distinct wrongs are bundled under one word and they do not always occur together. The first concerns the transaction. A buyer with no alternative is not really agreeing to a price; they are accepting a demand, and the freedom that makes exchange morally attractive is absent. This objection applies with particular force where the good is a necessity, and it explains why monopoly in water or medicine provokes a reaction that monopoly in luxuries does not. The second concerns power beyond the market. A firm that controls something everybody needs acquires leverage over suppliers, over employees, and over the political process, and that leverage is exercised in domains where the ordinary justification of profit has no application. Justice is concerned with concentrated power regardless of whether prices happen to be low. The third concerns what is foreclosed. Where a dominant firm can exclude rivals, the loss is not only present output but the alternatives that were never developed, and those are invisible in any measurement. An argument based on current prices therefore misses exactly what matters most. These objections come apart in practice. A firm may hold an enormous share while charging little, which defeats the first objection while leaving the second and third intact, and much recent argument about large technology companies turns on precisely this. Where the law defines the wrong purely as high prices, such firms are unreachable. What follows is that the moral case against concentration is broader than the economic one, and framing the whole question as a matter of consumer price concedes most of the ground before the argument starts.

subject: 항복한 적에 대한 의무
title: What is owed to somebody who has stopped fighting
content: A combatant who surrenders passes from one moral category into another. A moment earlier they could be attacked; now they may not be, and the change occurs without anything altering except their expressed intention. Understanding why this transformation is so absolute reveals what the permission to attack rested on in the first place. The standard account ties liability to threat. Combatants may be attacked because they pose a danger, not because they are guilty, since most soldiers on both sides are conscripts who did not choose the war. Once somebody has laid down their weapons they pose no danger, so the ground of the permission has vanished. Killing them is therefore not a lesser wrong than killing a civilian; it is the same wrong. This explains features of the rule that otherwise seem odd. It applies regardless of what the surrendering party did earlier, since the question is present threat rather than past conduct. It applies where taking prisoners is inconvenient, expensive, or dangerous, and the historical record contains a great many killings excused by exactly those difficulties. And it applies to those incapacitated by wounds, who have not surrendered but equally pose no threat. The obligation extends beyond not killing. A captor has taken somebody into their power and thereby assumed responsibility for their survival, so food, shelter, and medical care are owed rather than granted, and the reasoning is the same that applies to anybody who renders another helpless. What makes the rule fragile in practice is that it must be observed by people who were being shot at minutes earlier, and no argument reaches somebody in that state. This is why armies that maintain the rule do so through training and command rather than through moral instruction, and why its collapse in a unit is a failure of institution rather than of individual character.

subject: 간다라 미술이 만난 두 전통
title: Where two artistic worlds met in stone
content: In the region spanning parts of modern Pakistan and Afghanistan, sculpture produced during the first several centuries of our era shows an unusual combination. The subjects are Buddhist, drawn from an Indian religious tradition, while the treatment of drapery, of anatomy, and of facial features derives from Greek and Roman practice. This ancient meeting has occupied art historians since the material was first studied. The historical route by which these two traditions met is reasonably clear. Armies from the Mediterranean reached the region in the fourth century before our era, Greek speaking kingdoms persisted there for a long period afterwards, and later empires controlling the same ground maintained exchange with Rome. Consequently craftsmen working in the local tradition had access to models, and in some cases to workers, from a very different visual world. What resulted from this contact is not simple copying. The seated figure with folded legs is Indian; the heavy folds of cloth falling over the shoulder and the wavy hair are Mediterranean; and the combination produced a form that neither tradition would have generated alone. Some scholars argue that the earliest images of the Buddha in human form emerged here, since the older Indian practice had represented him through symbols rather than a body, although the claim is disputed by those who point to a rival centre further east. Their material record is extensive. Monasteries in the region held large sculptural programmes, and enough survives to trace changes across several centuries, including a gradual shift away from the classical treatment as local preferences reasserted themselves. Much of it has been destroyed or looted in recent decades. What the case demonstrates about ancient history is that contact between civilizations rarely produces a blend in equal parts. One tradition supplied the meaning and the other supplied the manner, and the result travelled onward to shape Buddhist art across the whole of eastern Asia.

subject: 미성년자를 어떻게 처벌할 것인가
title: Judging somebody who is not yet finished
content: Legal systems treat young offenders differently from adults, and the practice needs a justification rather than merely a tradition. The obvious answer is that children are less responsible, and stating why requires saying what responsibility depends upon and how it develops. One ground concerns understanding. Moral responsibility presupposes grasping what one is doing and what it means for others, and that grasp develops over years. A young child clearly lacks it, an adult clearly has it, and the intervening period is exactly where the difficulty lies, since the capacity arrives gradually and unevenly across different domains. A second ground concerns control. Evidence about development indicates that the capacity to resist impulse and to weigh distant consequences matures considerably later than the capacity to know that an act is wrong. An adolescent may understand perfectly well what they are doing while being less able to stop themselves, and responsibility tracks control as much as knowledge. A third ground concerns change. A young person is more likely to become somebody different, so a sentence that treats their present character as settled misdescribes them, and evidence on offending rates over the life course supports this strongly. Punishing on the assumption of permanence is therefore both unjust and empirically mistaken. Against these considerations stands the seriousness of some acts and the claims of those harmed by them. A victim's injury is not reduced by the age of whoever inflicted it, and systems that appear to treat serious harm lightly lose public support, which matters for whether they survive. What follows is that reduced responsibility is a genuine moral fact rather than a concession, and that acknowledging it does not require ignoring the harm. Separating what is owed to the victim from what may justly be imposed on the offender is the beginning of a defensible arrangement.

subject: 페트라의 물 관리
title: A city in the rock that never ran dry
content: Petra sits in a dry region receiving very little rain, in a landscape of sandstone gorges, and yet it supported a substantial population for centuries and was famous in the ancient world for its gardens. How a city in that position obtained water is the more remarkable achievement, and archaeology has largely reconstructed it. This ancient system began far outside the settlement. Springs in the surrounding hills were tapped and their water carried in channels cut along the rock face and in ceramic pipes, sloped carefully so that the flow neither scoured nor stagnated. Sections of pipe recovered from the site show a diameter chosen to keep the water moving under partial fill, which reduces the friction that a full pipe produces. Storage mattered to this civilization as much as delivery. Cisterns cut into the rock, sealed with plaster and covered against evaporation, held the winter rain, and dams across the side valleys diverted flash floods away from the inhabited gorges while directing the water into reservoirs. The same works therefore supplied the city and protected it, since a sudden flood through a narrow gorge is lethal. The wealth that paid for this came from position. The Nabataean kingdom controlled routes carrying incense north from Arabia, and a city able to water large caravans in that landscape held an advantage no rival could match. Water management was therefore not merely a civic amenity but the basis of the state's income. Decline in later centuries followed the routes rather than the engineering. When trade shifted toward sea transport and the region passed under other authorities, maintenance lapsed, an earthquake damaged the channels, and the population fell. What survives is a set of carved facades that visitors photograph, and behind them a hydraulic system that is the actual accomplishment of this ancient civilization.

subject: 도덕은 구성되는가 발견되는가
title: Whether moral truths are made or found
content: Two broad pictures compete in moral philosophy. On one, moral facts exist independently of what anybody thinks, and moral inquiry discovers them much as inquiry into the physical world discovers its facts. On the other, moral truths are constructed by the procedures through which reasonable people work out how to live together, and there is nothing further to find. The realist picture explains several features of moral practice well. We argue as though somebody might be wrong, we treat our own past views as mistaken rather than merely outgrown, and we think that a society approving of cruelty would be in error rather than simply different. Each of these makes straightforward sense if there is a truth being tracked. The difficulty is metaphysical and epistemic together. Moral facts, if they exist, must be very unlike other facts, since they cannot be observed and yet somehow bear on what we should do. Explaining how anybody comes to know them, and why our moral beliefs would be reliable about them, has proved persistently hard. The constructivist picture answers those difficulties. Moral truths arise from what agents committed to justifying themselves to one another would accept, so there is no mysterious realm and no puzzle about access. Its cost is that it seems to make the truths depend on us, and critics ask what happens where a procedure would endorse something monstrous. Constructivists reply by building constraints into the procedure, at which point the debate turns on whether those constraints are themselves constructed or found. What the exchange has established is that the two positions are less distant than they appear. Both agree that moral claims can be correct, both reject the view that anything goes, and their remaining disagreement concerns what makes a correct claim correct rather than whether any claim is.

subject: 잔인함 같은 두터운 개념
title: Words that describe and judge at once
content: Some moral vocabulary separates cleanly into description and evaluation. Saying an act caused suffering describes it; saying it was wrong evaluates it. Yet a great deal of our actual moral language does both at once, and words of this kind have attracted considerable philosophical attention because they resist the separation. Consider calling somebody cruel. The word tells you something factual — they inflict suffering, and they do so without the reluctance a decent person would feel — and it condemns them in the same breath. You cannot use it neutrally, and you cannot state its descriptive content without the condemnation coming along. Courage, generosity, betrayal, and honesty behave similarly. The philosophical interest lies in what such words show about moral judgment. If evaluation could always be peeled away from description, then moral disagreement would concern only the evaluative remainder, and the facts could be settled first. Thick concepts suggest otherwise, since two people who disagree about whether an act was cruel are disagreeing about the facts and about their significance simultaneously, and neither part can be settled without the other. This bears on a familiar claim that facts and values occupy separate domains. Somebody committed to that separation must treat thick terms as compounds to be analysed, and the analyses proposed have generally failed to capture how the words are actually used. The alternative is to accept that some descriptions are evaluative all the way down. What follows for practice is that moral argument frequently proceeds through such words rather than through abstract principles. Showing somebody that a practice they defend is properly called cruel does more work than any appeal to a general theory, because the word carries the judgment inside the description, and accepting the description is already accepting most of the argument.

subject: 서사시의 구연과 기억술
title: How singers held whole epics in memory
content: Long narrative poems were performed from memory in many cultures before writing, and the length of some of them provoked a question that seemed unanswerable: how could anybody retain tens of thousands of lines? Fieldwork among singers who still practised the art supplied the answer, and it changed how the ancient epics are understood. Researchers recording performers in the Balkans in the twentieth century found that singers did not memorise a fixed text. They had absorbed a stock of formulaic phrases, each fitting a particular position in the metrical line, and they assembled the narrative during performance from those units. Consequently the same singer telling the same story twice produced different words while maintaining the plot, and neither version was the correct one. This explains features of the classical epics that had puzzled readers. Repeated phrases attached to characters, apparently redundant lines, and standard sequences describing arming or feasting are not weak writing but the machinery of oral composition, allowing the singer to sustain the metre while thinking ahead. Once recognised, such formulas can be counted, and their density in the surviving Greek epics is exactly what oral composition would produce. The finding altered what those texts are taken to be. They are not works by an author in the modern sense but the recording of a tradition at one moment, made when writing arrived and somebody chose to fix a performance. Arguments about authorship have never entirely settled, although the tradition's role is no longer disputed. What the whole episode illustrates is how an art form can be misread across centuries because its conditions were forgotten. Readers accustomed to books had been evaluating oral composition by standards belonging to writing, and the qualities they had marked as faults turned out to be the technique.

subject: 카롤링거 소문자의 개혁
title: The handwriting that saved the ancient books
content: During the late eighth and ninth centuries a new script spread across western Europe, promoted by scholars working under Charlemagne. It used clearly separated letters of even height, with spaces between words and a consistent set of forms, and it replaced a patchwork of regional hands that had grown increasingly difficult to read. This medieval reform had consequences far beyond calligraphy. The problem this medieval reform solved was practical, although its effects were not. Manuscripts produced in different regions had diverged so much that a book copied in one place could be nearly illegible in another, and the older habit of running words together without spaces made reading slow and error prone. A common clear script meant that a text copied anywhere could be read everywhere, which mattered enormously to a programme aimed at correcting church books and reviving learning across a wide territory. Because of its timing, this reform determined what survives from the ancient world. This was the period when monastic scriptoria copied classical Latin texts in quantity, and for a substantial number of ancient works the oldest surviving manuscript dates from this era rather than from antiquity. Books that were not copied during this window frequently disappeared, so the reform is part of why any of the ancient library reached later centuries at all. There is a further consequence of these medieval copies that few notice. When Italian humanists of the fifteenth century sought manuscripts of ancient authors, the copies they found were in this medieval hand, which they took to be the authentic ancient script. They imitated it in their own writing, printers cut type based on those letterforms, and the lower case alphabet used across the world today descends from that misunderstanding. A reform intended to make ninth century books legible determined the shape of most printed text ever since.

subject: 정원 설계라는 시간의 예술
title: A design that is finished decades later
content: A garden is the only major art form whose material continues changing after the artist stops working. A painting is complete when the painter leaves it; a garden planted today will not show what was intended for twenty years, and by then the designer may be dead. Every decision therefore addresses a state of things that nobody present will see. Designers work with predicted form rather than present appearance. A tree placed for the shape it will hold at maturity looks wrong for a decade, and a planting that looks complete on the day it goes in will be overcrowded within a few seasons. Consequently the drawings made by garden designers show a future condition, and clients must be persuaded to accept something that will look sparse and awkward for years. Time enters the aesthetic in a second way. A garden is designed to be different in each season, so the work has four appearances rather than one, and a tradition may value a bare structure in winter as highly as summer abundance. Certain traditions extend this further, valuing the accumulated moss, the weathering of stone, and the settling of a design into its ground, none of which can be installed. Maintenance is therefore part of the work rather than its upkeep. A garden left alone does not remain as designed; it becomes something else within a few years, and the intention survives only through continuous intervention by people who understand it. This is why historic gardens are so difficult to conserve, since preserving them means neither freezing nor abandoning but continuing a practice. What the art demonstrates is a different relationship between maker and object. The designer initiates a process rather than producing a thing, and the finished work belongs partly to whoever tends it afterwards, which is an authorship that few other arts share.

subject: 보편화 가능성의 요구
title: Asking whether everybody could do it
content: A recurring test in moral thinking asks whether the principle behind an action could be adopted by everybody. If universal adoption would be impossible, or would defeat the purpose the actor had, the action is condemned. The test appears in many traditions and in ordinary conversation, and stating precisely what it establishes is harder than applying it. One reading treats the test as concerning practical contradiction. Consider somebody making a promise they intend to break. If everybody did this, promising would collapse as an institution, and the deceiver's own plan depends on the institution existing, so the principle cannot be universalised without destroying what makes it work. This form of the argument is powerful where it applies, although its scope is narrower than its defenders sometimes claim. A second reading concerns fairness rather than contradiction. Somebody making an exception for themselves is claiming a standing that others lack, and the test exposes this by asking what entitles them. Read this way the argument is about equal treatment, and it explains why the objection feels apt even where universal adoption would be perfectly possible. A familiar difficulty concerns how the principle is described. Almost any action can be described so specifically that universalising it is harmless, since nobody else is in exactly those circumstances. The test therefore depends on choosing the right level of description, and nothing within the test supplies that choice, which is its most serious weakness. What survives the criticism is a discipline rather than an algorithm. Asking what rule one is acting on, and whether one could state it publicly and accept others acting on it, exposes a great deal of self serving reasoning. It does not decide hard cases by itself, and treating it as though it did has produced some confident conclusions that will not bear examination.

subject: 탈춤의 풍자와 사회
title: Masked dance that mocks those in charge
content: Korean masked dance drama developed largely outside the court, performed at festivals by troupes drawn from the ordinary population, and its content is startlingly direct. Corrupt officials, hypocritical monks, and arrogant aristocrats are ridiculed by name and by type, and the audience is invited to laugh at exactly the people who ordinarily commanded deference. The masks make this possible. A performer wearing a face that is not their own occupies a position outside ordinary accountability, and the tradition regards what is said in performance as belonging to the character rather than to the person. Consequently criticism that would be dangerous in speech becomes permissible in an art form, and the same mechanism appears in masked traditions elsewhere. The masks themselves are exaggerated, frequently distorted, and their carving is part of the satire. Performance conditions reinforce the licence. These plays were staged outdoors, in the round or with the audience surrounding three sides, at festivals where ordinary rules were relaxed, and audience members shouted responses throughout. The occasion was already one of licensed reversal, so the drama's content matched the day rather than intruding upon it. The satire is not merely aggressive. Several traditional pieces devote as much attention to domestic conflict, particularly to the relations between a man, his wife, and his concubine, and the treatment of the wronged wife is sympathetic in a way that the surrounding culture's formal literature was not. The form therefore gave voice to positions with no other public expression. Preservation has changed the art. Now designated as cultural heritage and performed for audiences that include tourists, the plays are staged in conditions unlike those they were made for, and the satire lands differently when the officials mocked have been gone for a century. Practitioners disagree about whether the tradition should be kept as it was or allowed to address the present.

subject: 광고 이미지의 수사학
title: How a picture makes an argument
content: An advertisement rarely states a claim that could be disputed. It shows a scene, and the audience draws a conclusion that the advertiser never asserted, which is why analysing such images requires attending to what they imply rather than to what they say. The techniques involved are consistent enough to be catalogued. Association is the most basic. Placing a product beside something already valued transfers the value without any argument being offered, and no connection between the two need exist. The audience does not conclude that the product causes the desirable thing; they simply come to feel about one as they feel about the other, and that feeling is what the image was constructed to produce. Absence does further work. What is not shown carries meaning, since a picture of a meal without a kitchen, or of a garment without the labour that made it, presents the object as though it had arrived without a history. Critics of the form have long argued that this removal is the ideological content of commercial imagery, and the argument does not require any conspiracy, since the convention simply produces images that show ends without means. The gaze is a third element. Whether a figure looks out at the viewer or away, whether the viewpoint is above or below, and whether the body is presented whole or fragmented all position the audience in a relation to what is shown. Traditions of analysis developed for painting apply directly here, since the visual grammar is inherited from a much older tradition of picture making. What follows is that reading such images is a skill worth teaching. The argument an advertisement makes is unstated and therefore unavailable for objection, and naming the technique restores the possibility of disagreeing with it, which is precisely what the form is designed to prevent.

subject: 숭고와 아름다움의 구분
title: Two ways of being overwhelmed
content: Eighteenth century writers on aesthetics drew a distinction that has proved durable. Beauty, on their account, involves proportion, smoothness, and a scale the mind can take in comfortably, producing a settled pleasure. The sublime involves vastness, obscurity, and power, producing something closer to awe mixed with fear, and the two responses are not degrees of one thing. The distinction was drawn to explain an experience that a theory of beauty alone could not handle. A storm at sea, a mountain range, or an enormous ruin gives pleasure of a kind, and yet nothing about the pleasure resembles the satisfaction of a well proportioned face. The proposed explanation was that the sublime arises where something exceeds our capacity to grasp it while we remain safe from it, so the mind registers its own limit without being harmed. This had immediate consequences for art. Landscape painting shifted toward subjects that earlier taste had regarded as merely unpleasant — precipices, storms, and wilderness — and travellers began seeking exactly the scenery that previous generations had crossed with dread. The change in taste followed the theory as much as the theory described the change, which is unusual in the history of aesthetics. Later writers extended the idea. Some located the sublime not in the object but in the mind's discovery that it can conceive what it cannot perceive, which relocates the experience from nature to reason. Twentieth century thinkers applied the term to art that presents the unrepresentable, and the concept has been used to discuss catastrophe and modern scale. What makes the distinction valuable is that it separates two things ordinary language merges. Calling a mountain beautiful describes the response poorly, since the reaction includes something that comfort cannot contain, and a vocabulary with only one term for aesthetic pleasure had been forcing very different experiences into one word.

subject: 한자 동맹 창고의 운영
title: Warehouses that governed a northern sea
content: From the thirteenth century a network of trading towns around the Baltic and North Sea acted together, negotiating privileges, enforcing agreements, and occasionally making war. The Hanseatic League had no capital, no permanent army, and no single ruler, and it dominated northern commerce for roughly three centuries. Its instrument through the medieval centuries was the warehouse. Member merchants operating in a foreign port lived and traded from a walled compound holding storage, lodging, offices, and a chapel, and residence there came with rules governing conduct, weights, and dealings with outsiders. Such a compound in London, another in Bergen, and others in Novgorod and Bruges gave the association a physical presence in each market without requiring any territory. What held this medieval network together was the threat of exclusion. A town or a merchant who broke an agreement could be cut off from the whole system, losing access to markets across a wide region, and that sanction operated without any court or standing force. Consequently the arrangement functioned as a self enforcing set of agreements among parties who could not compel one another directly. Their cargoes were bulk rather than luxury: salt, grain, timber, fish, wax, and cloth, moved in quantity by ships built for capacity rather than speed. Preserved fish from northern waters, salted with salt from further south, fed inland populations during the medieval centuries, and the trade linked regions that had little else in common. Its decline came in later centuries as territorial states grew stronger. Rulers who could enforce their own rules had less use for an association of towns, and merchants from other regions entered the same routes with support that the league could not match. The compounds were closed one by one, and by the seventeenth century the arrangement survived only in name.
